nameStory: The orange peel fungus gets its name from an uncanny resemblance to discarded orange peels scattered on the forest floor. When you spot these bright orange, cup-shaped fungi, they look so much like citrus rinds that you might do a double-take wondering who's been snacking in the woods!
description: Orange peel fungus is a bright orange, cup-shaped fungus that literally looks like someone tossed orange peels onto the ground. These eye-catching fungi are part of the ascomycete group, which means they produce spores in tiny sacs rather than on gills like mushrooms. The cups start small and can grow to several inches across, maintaining their vivid orange color throughout their development. They're one of the most recognizable fungi you'll encounter in New England forests.

idTips.label: Cup Shape
idTips.description: Perfect cup or bowl shape that's deeply concave, like someone carved out a small orange bowl - the edges may be slightly wavy but maintain the cup form

idTips.label: Bright Orange Color
idTips.description: Vibrant orange color that's remarkably similar to an orange peel - the outside may be slightly paler or more peachy than the brilliant inner surface

idTips.label: Smooth Texture
idTips.description: Inner surface feels smooth and slightly waxy to the touch, while the outer surface has a more matte, fuzzy texture that's barely noticeable

idTips.label: Ground Growth
idTips.description: Always found growing directly from soil or leaf litter, never on wood - they seem to pop up from nowhere like scattered fruit rinds

idTips.label: Fragile Structure
idTips.description: Delicate and brittle - they'll crack or crumble easily when handled, much more fragile than actual orange peel

idTips.label: No Stem
idTips.description: Sits directly on the ground with no visible stem, though there may be a small attachment point at the base of the cup

habitat: Look for orange peel fungus in disturbed soil areas throughout New England's forests, particularly along trails, in clearings, or where the ground has been recently disturbed. They favor rich, organic soil and often appear in both deciduous and mixed forests. You'll frequently find them in areas where leaves have been cleared away or the soil has been compacted by foot traffic.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in spring as conditions are usually too cool and wet for optimal fruiting.
seasonality.summer: Occasional appearances during warm, humid periods, especially after summer rains create ideal moisture conditions.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for orange peel fungus - the cool, moist conditions of autumn provide perfect growing conditions and they're most commonly spotted from September through November.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent during winter months as freezing temperatures prevent growth and development.

funFact: Orange peel fungus can actually grow back from the same spot if you carefully break off just the visible cup part - the underground fungal network remains intact and can produce new fruiting bodies within days under the right conditions!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with actual orange peels! The dead giveaway is location and attachment - real orange peels will be loose and moveable, while orange peel fungus is firmly attached to the soil. Also, the fungus has a more uniform color and perfect cup shape compared to the irregular, segmented appearance of citrus peels.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'orange peel fungus,' this species has no relationship to citrus fruits whatsoever - it's purely a visual coincidence that created this perfect common name. The scientific name 'Aleuria aurantia' comes from Latin, with 'aurantia' meaning 'golden' or 'orange-colored.'
compareHints: Orange peel fungus is the only species in its genus Aleuria found in New England, making identification relatively straightforward. Within the broader cup fungus family, it's distinguished from similar species like scarlet cup fungus by its larger size, ground-growing habit, and distinctive orange (rather than red) coloration. Unlike many other cup fungi that grow on wood, orange peel fungus is consistently terrestrial.
